sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of an incomplete, crushed skull with displaced postorbital bones and an almost complete lower jaw. It also includes scattered plates forming the scleral ring and two elements of the hyoid bone. No soft tissue or keratinous parts are preserved.

In 2012, researchers estimated the wingspan of this small pterosaur to be around 2 meters. However, in 2023, the same team revised this estimate to between 3 and 4 meters, classifying it as a mid-sized pterosaur.
Romain Vullo and colleagues reported a new pterosaur skull from Las Hoyas in 2012. The genus and species Europejara olcadesorum were named that same year by Vullo et al.
The site was discovered in 1985 and yielded over 20,000 fossils by 2023.

In 2013, Mark Witton described tapejarids as adaptable, generalist fliers comparable to modern parrots and crows. Tapejarids likely flew in inland areas due to their short wings, while their long, well-muscled limbs aided in launching and flapping. They are thought to have been frugivorous or granivorous based on their short skulls, shaped jaws, and lack of teeth.
Researchers suggest it was frugivorous or granivorous and played a role in seed dispersal when angiosperms first appeared.

In 2012, Vullo and colleagues classified Europejara as a member of the pterosaur family Tapejaridae. In 2016, Rubi Vargas Pêgas and colleagues identified Europejara as the sister group to the Brazilian genera Caiuajara, Tapejara, and Tupandactylus. In 2019, Alexander W. Kellner and colleagues named the tribe Tapejarini to include Europejara and its Brazilian relatives.

Europejara lived in Spain during the Barremian age of the Early Cretaceous, 125 to 121 million years ago. It lived in a subtropical wetland environment represented by the La Huérguina Formation. The locality belongs to the La Huérguina Formation and dates to the late Barremian of the Early Cretaceous. Europejara lived during the Barremian age in Spain, indicating that tapejarids were distributed across Gondwana and Laurasia earlier than previously known. Europejara was recovered from the Las Hoyas site in the La Huérguina Formation, dated to the late Barremian of the Early Cretaceous.

It is debated whether tapejarids originated in Laurasia or Gondwana, with some researchers arguing that the monophyly of Chinese tapejarines does not support a Laurasian origin. More research is needed to support interpretations regarding the dispersal patterns and origins of tapejarids, including the relationship of Europejara to South American taxa. Researchers cautioned that more fossils and gut-content analysis are needed to determine if tapejarids co-evolved with angiosperms or merely dispersed them incidentally.
